blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A construct is an abstract characteristic that cannot be observed directly. It is inferred from measurable indicators (questionnaire items, test scores, observed behaviours) that theory says should reflect it.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Weight is not a construct: you put a person on a scale and read a number. “Quality of life”, “anxiety”, “trust in the health system” or “knowledge of CBHI benefits” cannot be read off any instrument. Researchers capture them indirectly. They ask a chosen set of questions, each an indicator, and combine the answers into a score that stands in for the construct.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: “Patient satisfaction” at a PHC is a construct. A questionnaire might ask ten questions (was the waiting time acceptable? were staff respectful? were explanations clear? would you recommend this facility?) and combine the answers into one satisfaction score.

points.html: Constructs differ from directly observed variables (age, weight, blood pressure; recall §1.1). A construct needs a whole instrument, and a body of evidence, before you can trust that its score reflects the intended idea.

Constructs that sound alike can be distinct: “patient satisfaction”, “quality of care” and “trust in provider”. Showing that an instrument measures the specific construct intended, and not an overlapping one, is the job of construct validity (§16.2.4).
